newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso strengthened by re-election vote.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso strengthened by re-election vote.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso emerged on Wednesday strengthened by a victory in Congress and one step closer to fulfilling his dream of being the first re-elected leader of Latin America's largest country.

Newspapers and commentators said Cardoso has passed the toughest test of his political life on Tuesday evening when the Chamber of Deputies approved a change to the constitution that would allow him to run again in the 1998 elections.

The bill must pass through the lower house again and then twice through the Senate, each time winning a 60 percent majority. It also faces a series of amendments on Wednesday morning that the government must defeat.
But commentators said the first vote was the most crucial.

"Cardoso succeeded in passing the first and most difficult test. It was a significant victory for the government, which expects the passage of the bill through its next stages to be more tranquil," wrote the financial daily Gazeta Mercantil.

In a tense ballot, 336 deputies voted to approve the constitutional amendment that would allow sitting presidents, governors and mayors to run for second consecutive terms for the first time since the republic was established in 1889.
The result was well above the 308 votes needed and represented a crushing defeat for Cardoso's foes, many of whom belonged to parties nominally allied to the government.
Political scientist Bolivar Lamounier, writing in Gazeta, noted that Cardoso's prestige over Congress had soared.

"As long as he remains highly popular and the strongest candidate for his own succession, parliamentarians will find it much more advantageous to cuddle up to the government than to distance themselves," Lamounier said.
Brazil has banned re-election since the founding of the republic because of fears of a revival of past imperial powers.

But Cardoso argues the economic reforms he launched as finance minister in 1994 that have brought inflation down from 5,000 percent a year to just 10 percent in 1996 need political continuity to prosper.
The second-round vote in the lower house is expected around Feb. 15, after the upcoming Carnival holiday season. The Senate votes are not yet scheduled but will also be after the holiday.

If he wins the next votes in Congress, he will join presidents Carlos Menem of Argentina and Alberto Fujimori of Peru as Latin American leaders who have rewritten their countries constitutions to allow their own re-elections.

Cardoso's desire to run again has dominated the Brazilian political agenda for months, effectively paralysing progress of essential reforms of the bloated civil service, the bankrupt social security system and of taxation legislation.
The financial markets, which had priced in a re-election victory, hope the passage of the bill will add impetus to Congress' deliberations over the economic reforms.
"The result might, or so it is hoped, free the country from the inaction in which it finds itself," wrote the Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper in an editorial.
Others were less optimistic, predicting the Brazilian government would now rest on its laurels, especially with the annual Carnival looming.
